title: YOU PRAYED THE SINNER’S PRAYER… BUT WHAT IF JESUS SAYS, “I NEVER KNEW YOU”?
paragraphs: YOU PRAYED THE SINNER’S PRAYER… BUT WHAT IF JESUS SAYS, “I NEVER KNEW YOU”?
The terrifying difference between repeating a prayer and truly belonging to Christ—and the beautiful hope for anyone who wonders whether their salvation is real.
Not because Jesus is speaking to atheists.
Not because He is confronting people who openly reject God.
But because He is describing people who call Him Lord.
People who sound religious. People who have done things in His name. People who are absolutely convinced that heaven is their destination.
And then comes a sentence so devastating that it should shake every ounce of false confidence we have ever placed in ourselves.
“I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity.” — Matthew 7:23 (KJV)
Read that again.
He did not say, “I knew you once, but I forgot you.”
He did not say, “You did not pray enough.”
He said, “I never knew you.”

Imagine standing before Jesus Christ, carrying a lifetime of church attendance, Christian photographs, worship playlists, religious posts, ministry activities, and a memory of the day you raised your hand at an altar call.
You remember the preacher saying, “Repeat after me.”
You remember closing your eyes.
You remember the words.
“Lord Jesus, I know I am a sinner. Come into my heart. Forgive me. Save me.”
Maybe you cried.
Maybe your family celebrated.
Maybe someone told you, “Congratulations. You are now saved.”
And perhaps something genuinely beautiful happened that day.
But here is the question almost nobody wants to ask.
Did you surrender your life to Jesus Christ, or did you merely repeat words about surrendering?
Because there is a difference.
An eternal difference.
And before you become frightened, defensive, or tempted to question every moment of your Christian life, please stay with me.
This is not an article written to convince genuine believers that Jesus is eager to reject them.
It is written because Jesus loves people too much to leave them resting in a false assurance.
And because the same Savior who warns us about empty religion also promises never to cast out the person who truly comes to Him (John 6:37).
That promise matters just as much as the warning.
Maybe you grew up in church.
Maybe your mother prayed over you before you could even pronounce the name of Jesus.
Maybe you attended Sunday school, memorized Bible verses, joined youth fellowships, and learned when to raise your hands during worship.
Maybe you have always identified yourself as Christian.
But somewhere along the way, your relationship with Jesus became a collection of religious habits rather than a life of trusting Him.
You knew the songs.
You knew the language.
You knew how to look spiritual.
But alone, when nobody could see you, you were carrying sins you had never honestly brought before God.
And eventually, you began wondering whether the prayer you prayed years ago was enough to cover a life you never really wanted Christ to change.
Or perhaps your story is different.
Perhaps you sincerely came to Jesus years ago, but lately you have fallen into sin, struggled with temptation, or endured a season of spiritual exhaustion.
You love Him, yet you are afraid.
You wonder whether your weakness means your salvation was never real.
If that is you, please understand something before we go any further.
The Gospel is not that strong Christians save themselves by performing better. The Gospel is that Jesus Christ saves sinners by grace.
The question is not whether you have become perfect.
The question is whether your hope is resting in the perfect Savior.
So what about the sinner's prayer?
Is it biblical?
Can God save someone who prays it?
And is saying it enough to make someone a Christian?
The answer is both simpler and more searching than many people expect.
A sinner's prayer can be a genuine expression of saving faith. But the act of repeating a prayer does not, by itself, make someone a Christian.
There is no biblical formula in which particular words automatically produce regeneration.
Salvation is not a spiritual transaction activated by the correct sentence.
It is not a password into heaven.
It is not a ritual that forces God to declare someone saved regardless of what that person actually believes.
Salvation is God's gracious work through Jesus Christ, received through faith.
Listen to the Apostle Paul.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” — Ephesians 2:8–9 (KJV)
The original Greek gives us an important window into Paul's meaning.
Τῇ γὰρ χάριτί ἐστε σεσῳσμένοι διὰ πίστεως
Tē gar chariti este sesōsmenoi dia pisteōs.
“For by grace you have been saved through faith.”
The word χάριτι (chariti) comes from charis, meaning grace or favor.
And πίστεως (pisteōs) comes from pistis, meaning faith, trust, or belief.
Paul does not say that we are saved by accurately repeating a particular prayer.
He says we are saved by grace through faith.
The Greek expression ἐστε σεσῳσμένοι (este sesōsmenoi) combines the verb “you are” with a perfect passive participle, emphasizing a salvation accomplished with an abiding result.
The emphasis is on what God has done, not on our ability to manufacture salvation through religious performance.
Even the most emotional prayer cannot purchase what only the blood of Jesus Christ can provide.
And even the simplest, trembling cry of genuine faith can be heard by the Savior who came to seek and save the lost.
Think about the criminal crucified beside Jesus.
His hands were nailed to a cross.
He had no opportunity to attend a discipleship class.
No chance to be baptized before his death.
No years of Christian service to present as evidence of a transformed life.
No polished sinner's prayer to recite.
He simply turned to Jesus and said:
“Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom.” — Luke 23:42 (KJV)
And Jesus answered:
“Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.” — Luke 23:43 (KJV)
What saved that dying man?
Not the length of his prayer.
Not the eloquence of his words.
Not his religious accomplishments.
He turned in faith toward the crucified King who could save him.
And that King welcomed him.
Do not miss the beauty of this.
The man could not climb down from his cross and repair his reputation.
He could not undo the harm he had caused.
He could not produce decades of visible good works.
But he could entrust himself to Jesus.
And Jesus was enough.
The power was never in the words of the sinner. The power was in the Savior to whom the sinner turned.
This is why Romans 10:9–10 must be understood carefully.
Paul writes:
The Greek text speaks of confessing Jesus as Lord:
κύριον Ἰησοῦν (kyrion Iēsoun)
And believing in the heart:
πιστεύσῃς ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ σου (pisteusēs en tē kardia sou)
The word kyrion identifies Jesus as Lord, while the verb pisteusēs refers to believing or trusting.
Paul is not offering a mechanical formula in which audible words save someone apart from genuine faith.
He is describing faith in the risen Christ that openly acknowledges Him.
The same chapter declares:
“For whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.” — Romans 10:13 (KJV)
That is a glorious promise.
But calling upon Jesus in faith is not the same thing as using His name while remaining unwilling to trust Him.
Jesus Himself asks:
“And why call ye me, Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say?” — Luke 6:46 (KJV)
Those words are uncomfortable.
Especially when we remember how easily Christianity can become part of our public identity without becoming the center of our private lives.
A person can know Christian vocabulary without knowing Christ.
A person can wear a cross without carrying one.
A person can post Bible verses without submitting to the God who inspired them.
A person can become familiar with the atmosphere of worship while remaining unfamiliar with repentance.
And yes, a person can pray the sinner's prayer without truly believing the Gospel.
But there is another danger we must avoid.
We must not turn salvation into an endless examination of whether our faith has been emotional enough, dramatic enough, or flawless enough.
The person who belongs to Christ may still struggle.
A genuine believer may stumble terribly.
Peter denied Jesus three times.
David committed grievous sin.
Thomas wrestled with doubt.
The Corinthian church had serious spiritual problems.
Yet Scripture does not teach that every failure proves a person has never been saved.
It teaches us to repent, return to Christ, and depend on His grace.
The difference between genuine faith and empty profession is not that one person never sins while the other does.
It is that genuine faith belongs to the Savior who forgives sinners and transforms them.
And that brings us to a word many modern Christians would rather avoid.
Repentance.
When Jesus began proclaiming the Gospel, Mark 1:15 records His message:
“Repent ye, and believe the gospel.”
In Greek:
μετανοεῖτε καὶ πιστεύετε ἐν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ
Metanoeite kai pisteuete en tō euangeliō.
“Repent and believe in the gospel.”
The verb μετανοεῖτε (metanoeite) calls for repentance, a change of mind and orientation toward God.
Biblical repentance is more than feeling embarrassed because someone discovered your sin.
It is more than crying because your choices produced painful consequences.
It involves turning toward God with a changed understanding of sin and of His rightful claim upon your life.
And the verb πιστεύετε (pisteuete) calls for belief or trust in the Gospel.
Both are present imperatives in this passage, expressing Jesus' summons to respond to God's kingdom announcement.
Repentance and faith belong together in the biblical call to conversion.
Not because repentance earns forgiveness.
Not because your tears pay for your sins.
But because the Christ who saves us from sin is not someone we can genuinely embrace while deliberately insisting that sin must remain our master.
Imagine a man standing inside a burning house.
The smoke is filling his lungs.
The flames are spreading across the ceiling.
A rescuer breaks through the door and reaches for him.
The man cries, “Save me!”
But then he says, “You may rescue me, but I refuse to leave this house.”
Something is terribly wrong with that response.
The illustration has limits, because salvation is God's gracious work, not a reward for human effort.
But it reveals an important truth.
We cannot sincerely ask Jesus to rescue us from sin while treating our bondage as something we have an absolute right to preserve.
We come to Him as sinners who need mercy.
We come with empty hands.
And we come because He is worthy of our trust.
Perhaps that is where this becomes painfully personal.
Because you have been asking Jesus to forgive something you have been carefully planning to do again.
Perhaps you have been hiding a relationship that you know dishonors Him.
Perhaps bitterness has become so familiar that you no longer recognize how deeply it controls you.
Perhaps you have been performing Christianity in public while privately feeding an addiction, dishonesty, lust, pride, greed, or unforgiveness.
And now you are uncomfortable.
Not because someone has discovered your secret.
But because the Word of God is reaching the place where you thought nobody could see.
Yet hear this carefully.
Conviction is not an invitation to despair. It is an invitation to come into the light.
You do not have to clean yourself up before you come to Jesus.
You come to Jesus because you cannot cleanse yourself.
You do not wait until you are strong enough to conquer every temptation.
You bring your weakness to the One whose grace is sufficient.
You do not earn His love by proving you deserve it.
You receive the mercy purchased by His death and resurrection.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
What a promise.
Not “He might forgive.”
Not “He will consider forgiving you if your history is not too ugly.”
He is faithful and just to forgive those who confess their sins.
And the foundation of that forgiveness is Jesus Christ, the righteous One, whose atoning sacrifice is described in the following chapter (1 John 2:1–2).
There is a reason the Gospel is called good news.
Because if salvation depended upon our ability to maintain a flawless spiritual record, none of us would have hope.
Not the pastor.
Not the worship leader.
Not the person who has memorized entire books of Scripture.
Not the person who has prayed every morning for forty years.
All of us need the same Savior.
And all of us must come through the same grace.
Now consider one of the most misunderstood encounters in the Bible.
In John chapter 3, Nicodemus comes to Jesus.
He is not an openly rebellious outsider.
He is a Pharisee.
A teacher of Israel.
A man who understands religious traditions and the Scriptures.
If anyone could have presented an impressive religious résumé, Nicodemus could.
Yet Jesus tells him:
“Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.” — John 3:3 (KJV)
The Greek expression is:
γεννηθῇ ἄνωθεν (gennēthē anōthen)
The word ἄνωθεν (anōthen) can mean “again” or “from above,” and John's account uses this meaningful language to point toward the necessity of spiritual birth from God.
Jesus is not telling Nicodemus to become more religious.
He is telling him that something must happen which human religious achievement cannot produce.
He must be born from above.

That is why John 1:12–13 says those who receive Christ and believe in His name are given the right to become children of God, and that this birth is not ultimately produced by human ancestry or human will, but by God.
Christianity is not merely adopting a religious label.
It is not simply deciding to behave better.
It is not a ceremony that changes your public identity while leaving your spiritual condition untouched.
It is life received from God through Jesus Christ.
This is the wonder of the new birth.
And it explains why a prayer can accompany conversion without being the cause of conversion.
God saves.
Christ redeems.
The Holy Spirit gives life.
The sinner believes.
And the life that God gives begins to bear fruit.
That fruit matters.
But we must understand its place.
Ephesians 2:8–9 declares that we are saved by grace through faith, not by works.
Then verse 10 says:
“For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them.”
Notice the order.
We are not saved by good works.
We are saved for good works.
Obedience is not the price we pay to purchase salvation.
It is the fruit of the salvation God freely gives.
James 2:17 says:
“Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone.”
James is not contradicting Paul.
Paul rejects works as the basis of our justification before God.
James challenges the claim that a faith which produces no evidence of life should be treated as genuine.
One confronts the pride that tries to earn salvation.
The other confronts the presumption that claims salvation while remaining indifferent to the God who saves.
Both are necessary.
Both protect the Gospel.
And both lead us back to Jesus.
You see, there are two terrible lies that can destroy a person's spiritual life.
The first says, “I prayed once, so it does not matter how I live.”
The second says, “I still struggle, so Jesus could never truly love or save me.”
The Gospel destroys both lies.
Grace is not permission to remain enslaved to sin.
And spiritual weakness is not proof that Christ has abandoned everyone who struggles.
Romans 6:1–2 rejects the idea that grace gives believers permission to continue deliberately in sin.
But Romans 8:1 also declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
Do you see the balance?
Jesus does not save us because we have finally become good enough.
And Jesus does not save us so that we can make peace with the very sin from which He came to redeem us.
He saves us because He is merciful.
He changes us because He is Lord.
And He keeps us because He is faithful.
Perhaps you are remembering the day you prayed the sinner's prayer.
You were a child.
Or a teenager.
Or an exhausted adult sitting in the back row of a church.
Perhaps your voice shook.
Perhaps you did not understand every theological detail.
Perhaps you could barely find the words.
Does that mean your conversion was false?
Absolutely not.
You do not need perfect theological vocabulary to be saved.
You need the Savior proclaimed in the Gospel.
A child can genuinely trust Jesus.
A broken adult can genuinely trust Jesus.
A dying criminal can genuinely trust Jesus.
And someone who comes with trembling faith can be received by Him.
The issue is not whether your prayer sounded impressive.
The issue is whether you were truly looking to Christ in faith.
And if you realize today that your earlier prayer was only words, do not waste another moment trying to defend an empty religious memory.
Come to Jesus now.
Not because you need to manufacture a more emotional experience.
Not because you must repeat a prayer until you feel something supernatural.
But because Christ Himself is calling sinners to repent and believe.
There is a profound difference between trusting a memory of a prayer and trusting the living Savior.
Your assurance must ultimately rest on Jesus Christ and His promises, not on the intensity of a moment you once experienced.
First John 5:13 says:
“These things have I written unto you that believe on the name of the Son of God; that ye may know that ye have eternal life.”
God does not intend His children to spend their entire lives imprisoned by spiritual uncertainty.
The Scriptures offer genuine assurance to those who believe in Christ.
They also invite us to examine whether our profession is real.
Second Corinthians 13:5 says:
“Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith.”
That examination should lead us toward the truth, not toward endless fear.
Ask yourself whether you are trusting Jesus Christ or merely trusting that you performed a religious act.
Ask whether you are willing to acknowledge your sin before God or whether you are determined to defend it.
Ask whether your life shows any growing evidence of His work, however imperfect and gradual.
And when you discover weakness, do not immediately conclude that you are beyond hope.
Bring that weakness to Christ.
Because even the act of examining ourselves must happen in the light of His grace.
Now return with me to Matthew 7.
Those frightening words.
“I never knew you.”
There is something important we must notice.
The people Jesus describes appeal to their religious achievements.
“Have we not prophesied in thy name? and in thy name have cast out devils? and in thy name done many wonderful works?” — Matthew 7:22 (KJV)
Their defense is built around what they claim to have done.
Their spiritual résumé becomes their argument.
But Jesus exposes the tragedy of religious profession without genuine relationship and obedience.
And just before this warning, He says:
“Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven; but he that doeth the will of my Father which is in heaven.” — Matthew 7:21 (KJV)
This does not mean we earn entrance into heaven through sinless performance.
It means an empty profession cannot substitute for genuine faith that takes God's will seriously.
Jesus is exposing the difference between appearance and reality.
And there is a beautiful contrast elsewhere in Scripture.
In John 10:27–28, Jesus says:
“My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me: And I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish.”
There it is.
The frightening words of Matthew 7 are, “I never knew you.”
The comforting words of John 10 are, “I know them.”
And the Shepherd gives His sheep eternal life.
Not temporary life until their next failure.
Not conditional affection based on how impressive they look to others.
Eternal life.
The security of Christ's sheep rests in the Shepherd who knows them and holds them.
That is where our hope belongs.
Not in a perfect prayer.
Not in a perfect church attendance record.
Not in the number of people who admire our Christian posts.
In Jesus Christ.
The crucified and risen Son of God.
The One who bore our sins.
The One who conquered death.
The One who intercedes for His people.
The One who welcomes the repentant sinner.
The One who does not break a bruised reed or extinguish a smoldering wick (Matthew 12:20).
Maybe you have been carrying a secret fear for years.
You have been wondering whether you are truly saved.
Maybe you have never told anyone.
You smile when the pastor speaks about heaven.
You sing when everyone else sings.
But when the room becomes quiet, a question rises inside you.
“Lord, do I really belong to You?”
You do not need to answer that question by searching for an emotional feeling strong enough to silence every doubt.
Look to the Gospel.
Jesus Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, was buried, and rose again on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
He is the Son of God.
He is the risen Lord.
He is the only Savior.
And His invitation remains open.
John 6:37 says:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.”
What an astonishing promise.
The person who truly comes to Christ is not met with a locked door.
The broken are not told to return when their lives look respectable.
The ashamed are not required to erase their history before receiving mercy.
The guilty are not asked to purchase forgiveness.
Jesus calls them to Himself.
And the One who died for sinners is not unwilling to receive sinners.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
Not because sin was harmless.
Not because rebellion was acceptable.
Not because God's holiness could simply be ignored.
But because Jesus Christ entered our broken world, bore the judgment our sins deserved, and rose victorious so that sinners could be reconciled to God.
The cross tells the truth about how serious sin is.
The empty tomb announces how powerful our Savior is.
And grace tells us that our worst chapter does not have to be the final chapter.
Remember Peter.
He promised loyalty.
He declared that he would stand with Jesus even if others abandoned Him.
And then, in a courtyard filled with fear, he denied knowing his Lord.
Three times.
Imagine the shame.
Imagine hearing the rooster crow.
Imagine realizing that the One you loved had been betrayed by your own lips.
Luke 22:61 records that Jesus turned and looked at Peter.
Peter went outside and wept bitterly.
But Peter's story did not end in that courtyard.
After His resurrection, Jesus restored him and entrusted him with the care of His sheep (John 21:15–19).
The man who denied Christ became a witness to Christ.
Not because denial was a small matter.
Not because Peter deserved a second chance.
But because the risen Jesus is merciful.
That is the heart of our message.
He does not rewrite the past by pretending it never happened.
He redeems sinners by His grace and gives them a new future in Him.
Perhaps your scandal is known to everyone.
Perhaps it is known only to you.
Perhaps you have made mistakes that cost you relationships, opportunities, credibility, or years you can never recover.
Or perhaps your greatest struggle is not some dramatic public failure.
Perhaps it is the quiet, exhausting burden of trying to appear spiritually strong while feeling desperately empty.
Jesus sees both.
He sees the sinner who needs to repent.
And He sees the weary believer who needs to be strengthened.
His Gospel is sufficient for both.
So what should you do if you realize today that you have been trusting in a prayer rather than in Christ?
Come to Him.
Confess your sin.
Believe the Gospel.
Turn from your rebellion and entrust yourself to Jesus.
You can speak to Him in your own words.
You do not need to copy someone else's emotional experience.
But if you struggle to find words, perhaps this prayer expresses what your heart desires to say.

“Lord Jesus, I confess that I am a sinner and cannot save myself. I have trusted in religious words, appearances, and my own efforts when I should have been trusting in You. I believe that You died for sinners and rose again. Have mercy on me. Forgive my sins. Turn my heart away from rebellion and teach me to follow You. I do not want an empty religious identity. I want to know You and belong to You. My hope is not in the words I am praying, but in You, my crucified and risen Savior. Amen.”
And please understand this.
The prayer itself is not a guarantee of salvation.
Christ is the Savior.
If those words express genuine repentance and faith, they can be a meaningful way to call upon Him.
But never mistake the expression of faith for the object of faith.
Afterward, begin walking with Jesus.
Read His Word.
Pray.
Seek fellowship in a faithful local church.
Be baptized in obedience to Christ, according to the teaching and practice of your Christian community.
Learn from mature believers who can help you understand Scripture.
When you fall, confess your sin and return to Him.
When you are confused, seek biblical guidance.
When your feelings become unreliable, hold fast to God's promises.
And remember that spiritual growth is not always dramatic.
Sometimes transformation looks like confessing the truth after years of lying.
Sometimes it looks like walking away from temptation even while your heart is still fighting.
Sometimes it looks like asking someone for forgiveness.
Sometimes it looks like seeking help for a destructive habit.
Sometimes it looks like opening your Bible again after months of spiritual silence.
Sometimes it looks like whispering through tears, “Jesus, I still need You.”
Do not despise the small beginnings of a life being changed by grace.
And do not confuse slow growth with the absence of God's work.
He is patient with His children.
Yet His patience is never an invitation to become comfortable with sin.
It is a reason to return to Him with gratitude and renewed obedience.

If this article has exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to confess private details publicly. Bring them honestly before God, and where appropriate, seek help from a trusted pastor or mature believer.
And if you are unsure what you believe, you are welcome to ask an honest question.
You do not have to pretend to have everything figured out before you begin seeking the truth.
There are people in your life who may need to read this.
Someone who thinks a childhood prayer gives them permission to live without Christ.
Someone who is terrified that one failure means Jesus has abandoned them.
Someone who grew up in church but has never understood grace.
Someone who walked away from Christianity because all they encountered was religious performance.
Someone who believes their past is too shameful for redemption.
Because one article may begin a conversation.
But discipleship is a lifelong journey.
And that is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
We want people to move beyond religious appearances into a growing understanding of God's Word, a deeper trust in Jesus Christ, and a life increasingly shaped by the Gospel.
Those resources are intended to help believers grow in biblical understanding, strengthen their faith, and remain spiritually nourished.
And if this ministry has helped you, I want to invite you into something deeper than simply reading another article.
Not because a monthly payment is proof that you are saved.
And certainly not because you must pay money to glorify Jesus Christ.

You glorify God by trusting, loving, and obeying Him. Supporting Gospel-centered ministry can be one meaningful expression of that devotion, but it is never a requirement for salvation or spiritual worth.
Scripture encourages believers to give willingly, not under pressure.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
That is the spirit in which this invitation is offered.
These are small reminders of our gratitude for people who help make this work possible.
Think about the person scrolling alone tonight.
The father quietly ashamed of the way he has treated his family.
The mother who has prayed for years for her child to return to Christ.
The teenager who believes their life is already ruined.
The exhausted believer who has nearly stopped praying.
The person who calls themselves Christian but has never understood what it means to be born again.
The person who thinks Jesus could never forgive them.
We cannot know whose heart God may touch through a single message faithfully shared.
But we can keep proclaiming the truth.
We can keep opening Scripture.
We can keep pointing people away from self-righteousness and toward the crucified and risen Savior.
We can keep making resources available to people who are hungry for God's Word.
And with willing partners, we can continue and expand that work.
And whether or not you are able to give financially, you can still help.
Pray for this ministry.
Use the free library.
Engage in meaningful conversations about Scripture.
Encourage someone who is struggling.
And your inability to give does not make your love for God less genuine.
The Gospel must never become a product that people feel pressured to purchase.
It is good news to be proclaimed freely.
What we invite you to support is the ongoing work of sharing and teaching that good news.
It is about making Jesus Christ known.
And now, before you leave, I want to return to the question that brought us here.
Is saying the sinner's prayer enough to make someone a Christian?
No—not if we mean that merely repeating the words automatically saves someone.
A prayer can express genuine repentance and faith.
But the prayer is not the Savior.
Jesus is.
The words are not the foundation of salvation.
His finished work is.
And the evidence of genuine faith is not a sinless life, but a life increasingly shaped by the grace and lordship of Christ.
So if you have been relying only on the memory of a prayer, look to Jesus today.
If you have been running from God, turn to Him.
If you have been hiding sin, bring it into His light.
If you have been crushed by shame, remember the cross.
If you have been exhausted by trying to earn God's acceptance, remember grace.
If you have been terrified that your weakness is greater than His mercy, remember the empty tomb.
And if you truly belong to Jesus, do not spend your life staring only at the failures He has already called you to confess and forsake.
Lift your eyes to your Savior.
The One who began a good work in His people will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6).
The One who intercedes for those who come to God through Him is able to save completely (Hebrews 7:25).
The One who calls His sheep by name is the Shepherd who lays down His life for them (John 10:3, 11).
This is not a Gospel of empty words.
It is not a Gospel of religious pretending.
It is not a Gospel of trying desperately to make ourselves worthy.
It is the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
His righteousness.
His sacrifice.
His resurrection.
His mercy.
His lordship.
His grace.
And that grace is powerful enough to confront our deepest sin without destroying our hope.
Powerful enough to expose religious hypocrisy while welcoming the repentant.
Powerful enough to humble the proud and lift the broken.
Powerful enough to turn a persecutor named Saul into an apostle who proclaimed the Christ he once opposed.
Powerful enough to restore a denying disciple named Peter.
Powerful enough to welcome a dying criminal who had nothing left to offer.
And powerful enough to save every sinner who truly comes to Jesus Christ in faith.
So please, do not walk away from this article asking only, “Did I say the right words?”
Ask the greater question.
“Am I trusting the right Savior?”
Because when the final day comes, the hope of the Christian will not be, “Lord, remember how perfectly I prayed.”
It will be, “Lord Jesus, You are my only hope.”
And for those who belong to Him, that hope will never put them to shame (Romans 10:11).
Heaven is not opened by the prayer you managed to remember, but by the Savior who remembers those who belong to Him.
